body_markdown:
The organizations best prepared for coordinated manipulation treat it the way they treat cyber threats: as a standing risk with clear owners, defined processes, and board attention. That approach is spreading, and narrative intelligence is on its way to becoming as expected as cybersecurity. In June, Cyabra was named a Market Shaper in the 2026 Gartner® Emerging Market Quadrant for Narrative Intelligence - Startup Vendors, the first report to define this market.


TL;DR


- Gartner predicts that 45% of chief communications officers (CCOs) will adopt narrative intelligence technologies by 2029 to support reputation monitoring amid an intensifying disinformation landscape.
- Narrative intelligence is moving from periodic reporting into everyday security, crisis, and communications workflows.
- As adoption widens, the debate shifts from whether organizations need it to how it should be governed.
- Durable standards will rest on evidence: traceable signals of authenticity and coordination that any team can verify.


### Narrative Intelligence Is Following the Path Cybersecurity Took


Cybersecurity started as a specialist concern, handled by a small technical team and raised with leadership mostly after something went wrong. Over time, it became a standing function with owners, budgets, and board reporting. Few organizations would now consider operating without it.


Narrative Intelligence is moving along a similar path. Coordinated inauthentic activity affects how markets react, how audiences read a brand, and how the public interprets events. Generative AI keeps lowering the cost of producing that activity at scale. Gartner expects that “the narrative intelligence market will rapidly transition from providing passive, retrospective analysis to delivering autonomous management and remediation options.”


Cyabra identifies this as the same maturation curve security went through, from understanding what happened to acting while it is happening.


### Insight Has to Live Where Decisions Are Made


The report also anticipates where these capabilities will sit: “Organizations will increasingly mandate that the data and capabilities be integrated directly into their security operations centers (SOCs), broader crisis management workflows and reputation management capabilities, treating cognitive attacks with the same urgency as cyberbreaches.”


For teams, this changes what narrative intelligence has to deliver. A retrospective report explains a campaign after it has already shaped perception. A standing function needs three things: early signals, evidence structured for the people who act on it, and a clear sense of scale so the response stays proportionate. Communications needs to know whether pressure is organic. Legal needs findings it can stand behind. Security needs to see how activity connects to other threats.


Cyabra’s evidence-based mitigation workflows are built for these needs, packaging findings in a form teams can act on inside the processes they already run.


### The Debate Moves From Whether to How


As adoption widens past early movers, the live questions change. Fewer organizations ask whether they need narrative intelligence. More ask how it should be governed: what counts as manipulation, how authentic and coordinated activity get told apart consistently, and what standards the field holds itself to.


These questions matter because the work touches public conversation. Cyabra’s position is that standards should rest on observable behavior: whether accounts are authentic, whether activity is coordinated, and how far it travels. Grounding analysis in behavior keeps it separate from judgments about which opinions are acceptable. It also makes findings testable. Every conclusion should trace back to evidence that a second analyst, a platform, or a legal reviewer could examine and confirm.


Cyabra intends to help shape those standards, drawing on years of investigations across sectors and regions.


### Each Sector Is Building a Permanent Capability


The shift looks different depending on who is exposed.


For enterprises, narrative intelligence is becoming part of brand security and a standing board-level topic. Manufactured backlash, astroturfed pressure, and coordinated campaigns around earnings or product launches all require the ability to separate real sentiment from orchestrated activity.


For defense and intelligence organizations, the information domain is permanent operating ground. Influence operations run continuously, ahead of elections, military events, and policy decisions, so the monitoring has to run continuously too.


For boards and investors, narrative exposure is becoming one more risk that well-run companies are expected to understand and report on.


### What Communications and Brand Teams Can Do Now


- **Assign ownership.** Decide which function owns narrative intelligence and narrative risk, and how it hands off to security, legal, and crisis teams.
- **Set a benchmark early.** Knowing what authentic conversation about your organization looks like makes coordinated deviations easier to spot.
- **Add narrative scenarios to crisis plans.** Treat a coordinated campaign as a defined incident type with its own escalation path.
- **Ask what evidence sits behind every alert.** Traceable findings hold up with legal teams, platforms, and boards.


Narrative intelligence is settling into the place security already holds. That is why we built Cyabra, restoring trust and authenticity for global enterprises and governments.
